To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Canada Basin is underlain by oceanic crust.
(1) the crustal thickness beneath the Queen Elizabeth Islands is about 30 km, and (2) the crust is oceanic rather than continental.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the seismic properties of the crust and uppermost mantle of the Arctic Basin and the continental shelves of the Arctic Archipelago.
the development of a method of seismic refraction profiling on sea ice.
the seismic structure of the continental shelf of the Queen Elizabeth islands of the Arctic Ocean.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the crust of the Queen Elizabeth Archipelago is oceanic in nature, but that the crust of Ellesmere Island is continental.
the crust of the Polar Continental Shelf is oceanic in character.

the crustal structure of the Polar Continental Shelf is oceanic, and that the crustal material is probably of oceanic origin, having been transported to its present location during the opening of the Canada Basin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the crustal model of the Arctic Ocean is similar to the oceanic model for the North Atlantic and the North Pacific.
the crustal model for the Queen Elizabeth Islands is similar to that of the Arctic Ocean and that it is similar to that for the continental crust.
the crustal thickness is 28 ±4 km at land, thinning to less than 15 km at the continental shelf-break and is probably oceanic rather than continental crust.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the seismic data from the Arctic shelf are of high quality, and can be interpreted in a similar fashion as data collected in more temperate climates.
seismic data recorded from sea ice are not necessarily of poor quality.
the seismic refraction profile is a useful tool to understand the crustal structure of the Arctic.
